title: Census unearthed: explore 50 years of change from 1961
meta_description: Article exploring ways in which how we live has changed in the 50 years between 1961 and 2011, presenting insights from the 1961 Census small area statistics compared with census data from 2011.

breadcrumb.text: Census unearthed: explore 50 years of change from 1961

lede: From having an inside toilet to how many of us are married, newly digitised data show how the ways we live changed from 1961 to 2011.

body.text: 9 August 2021
Life in England and Wales changed dramatically between 1961 and 2011, from the homes we live in to our relationships and everyday amenities.
Recently digitised data from the 1961 Census Small Area Statistics can show these changes in detail at a local level for the first time.
They also show how the picture provided by the census of people’s needs and lives has always been useful.
Explore how areas compared with each other with our interactive maps and see what changed in the 50 years up to 2011.

body.box_text: This article is produced with thanks to the [2,800 volunteers who made 5.5 million checks](https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/dataliberation/1961-census/about/research) to help turn scans of the 1961 Census Small Area Statistics into digital tables.

body.h2: In some areas of England and Wales in 1961, more than half of homes didn’t have an inside toilet
body.text: We take it for granted now that you have a flushing toilet at home but in 1961, indoor toilets were much less common.

body.h2: In some areas of England and Wales in 1961, more than half of homes didn’t have an inside toilet
body.text: The census that year asked if people had a toilet inside or attached to the home they were living in. Nearly 7% of households in England and Wales did not.

body.h2: In some areas of England and Wales in 1961, more than half of homes didn’t have an inside toilet
body.text: Outdoor toilets could be in a separate building in the garden, or in some cases, a communal toilet for the street.

body.h2: In some areas of England and Wales in 1961, more than half of homes didn’t have an inside toilet
body.text: In some rural districts, more than half of households had a toilet separate from their property.

body.h2: In some areas of England and Wales in 1961, more than half of homes didn’t have an inside toilet
body.text: Of the 1961 districts with the highest proportion of homes without inside or attached toilets, the top 50 were all rural areas, ranging from 39% of homes without a toilet in Teifiside in Wales, to as high as 59% in the area of Mitford and Launditch in Norfolk.

body.h2: In some areas of England and Wales in 1961, more than half of homes didn’t have an inside toilet
body.text: The 1961 Census also asked if households had a fixed bath with waste-water plumbing. Those who didn’t have a fixed bath sometimes had a table-top or standalone bath, filled and emptied by bucket or ladle from a water heater.

body.h2: In some areas of England and Wales in 1961, more than half of homes didn’t have an inside toilet
body.text: You can explore the results for both questions using the interactive maps. They display data on the map of England and Wales as it looked in 1961, so your area may look different to how it is today. The letters after place names are part of their description – a rural district (RD) is a distinct area from an urban district (UD) or a metropolitan or municipal borough (MB).

body.h2: Divorce has risen tenfold and fewer people are married
body.text: Divorce has risen tenfold and fewer people are married

body.h2: Divorce has risen tenfold and fewer people are married
body.text: At the time of the 1961 Census, 68% of people aged 16 years and over were married and 0.8% were divorced. In the 2011 Census, this had changed to 49% of people aged 16 years and over married or in a same-sex civil partnership, and 9% divorced or in a legally dissolved civil partnership.

body.h2: Divorce has risen tenfold and fewer people are married
body.text: Censuses are snapshots, so they can’t tell us how many times someone has been married or in a civil partnership but the differences between these figures for 1961 and 2011 reflect a period of stark social change.

body.h2: Divorce has risen tenfold and fewer people are married
body.text: By 2011, divorce law had become less stringent, civil partnerships for same-sex couples had existed for six years and people who were separated but legally married could record this on the census, options that were not available in 1961. To allow comparison between years, we have included separated but legally married people as “married” in 2011.

body.h2: More people owned a home in 2011 than 50 years before
body.text: More people owned a home in 2011 than 50 years before

body.h2: More people owned a home in 2011 than 50 years before
body.text: Renting was the norm for most households in 1961. Only 42% of households owned their own home, and in several areas of central London, home ownership was lower than 10%.

body.h2: More people owned a home in 2011 than 50 years before
body.text: By the time of the 2011 Census, 50 years on, home ownership had risen to 64%. The lowest home ownership was still in London areas, as they existed geographically in 1961, the very lowest being in the area that was the 1961 metropolitan borough of Shoreditch, at 16%.

body.h2: More people owned a home in 2011 than 50 years before
body.text: Who people rented from changed too. In 1961, 28% of households were private rented accommodation, and 24% of households rented from a local authority or New Town corporation.

body.h2: More people owned a home in 2011 than 50 years before
body.text: These [“New Towns”](https://www.parliament.uk/about/living-heritage/transformingsociety/towncountry/towns/overview/newtowns/) were part of efforts to meet housing shortages after the Second World War by building new settlements, such as Stevenage and Crawley. The developer corporations were dissolved, and rented homes handed over to local councils, which is why the category does not exist today.

body.h2: More people owned a home in 2011 than 50 years before
body.text: The introduction of the “Right to Buy” policy in 1980 allowed council tenants to buy the home they rented and, in some instances, council housing was replaced by properties owned by private landlords.

body.h2: More people owned a home in 2011 than 50 years before
body.text: By 2011, only 9% of homes were rented from a local authority and 15% of homes were in private rented accommodation.

body.h2: The population aged and rural areas became more urbanised
body.text: The population aged and rural areas became more urbanised

body.h2: The population aged and rural areas became more urbanised
body.text: Between 1961 and 2011, the population increased and became proportionally older. This was a result of increased life expectancy and declining birth rates.

body.h2: The population aged and rural areas became more urbanised
body.text: In nearly every area of England and Wales (97%), the proportion of people aged 75 years and over increased. The places with the biggest increases in residents aged 75 years and over were mostly in coastal areas of Norfolk and Suffolk. In Hunstanton (urban district), the proportion of older people increased from 6% to 23%.

body.h2: The population aged and rural areas became more urbanised
body.text: There are a few exceptions, such as in some parts of Sussex and London. In what was the municipal borough of Hove, the proportion of over-75-year-olds dropped from 11% to 7% between 1961 and 2011, and in Hastings county borough it went down from 10% to 8%.

body.text: Some of these were the [New Towns](https://www.parliament.uk/about/living-heritage/transformingsociety/towncountry/towns/overview/newtowns/), which included new settlements built between 1961 and 2011. These include Milton Keynes and Northampton, which account for the local areas with the largest increases in population in the 50 years.

body.h2: The population aged and rural areas became more urbanised
body.h4: Population has aged in most areas of England and Wales
body.h5: Explore 1961 areas by population age bands compared with 2011
body.text: Proportionally, the places with the biggest populations in England and Wales in 2011 were the same six urban districts as they were in 1961, as defined by historical 1961 boundaries: the cities of Birmingham, Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool, Sheffield and Bristol.

body.h2: The population aged and rural areas became more urbanised
body.h4: Population has aged in most areas of England and Wales
body.h5: Explore 1961 areas by population age bands compared with 2011
body.text: Of those six urban centres, five also saw the biggest reductions in the proportion of the population of England and Wales they were home to between censuses. The city of Birmingham, as it was defined in 1961, went from housing 2.4% of the population to 1.7%.

body.h4: Population has aged in most areas of England and Wales
body.h5: Explore 1961 areas by population age bands compared with 2011
body.text: Places that saw an increase in population proportion between censuses were generally areas that in 1961 were classed as rural districts. As cities spread, people moved and the New Towns were built, some of these previously rural districts became more urbanised.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: In most areas of England and Wales, people in 2011 lived in less crowded homes than in 1961, not in terms of space, but in terms of people.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: People filling out the census in 1961 and 2011 told us how many rooms they had and how many people lived in their home.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: We can use this to calculate “persons per room”, where rooms include kitchens and conservatories but not bathrooms and store cupboards or corridors.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: One person per room could mean one person in a single room, or 5 people in a 5-room house.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: It can’t tell us how much space each person has – one room may be a very small studio or a large kitchen-diner – but it does tell us we’re getting more spread out in how we live as households.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: Possible reasons for this are wide-ranging and include new housing reducing the need for multi-generational households, people having fewer children and older people living longer in family houses.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: Nearly every local area as they were in 1961 (over 99%) has seen an increase in the number of households in that area that have 1 person per room or less, showing households have more rooms available per person to live in.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: This is particularly pronounced in Kirkby urban district, which has seen a 38 percentage point (pp) increase in households with up to 1 person per room, a 27 pp reduction in households with 1 to 1.5 persons per room, and an 11 pp reduction in households with more than 1.5 persons per room.

body.h2: Households have fewer people per room in 2011 than 1961
body.text: Some areas have bucked this trend, where homes had more people per room. In a few areas, notably East Ham (Essex) county borough, Southall (Middlesex) and Leyton (Essex) municipal boroughs, there was an increase in the percentage of households that had between 1 and 1.5 persons per room compared with 1961, and also households with more than 1.5 persons per room.

body.h2: Be a part of it
body.text: Be a part of it

body.h2: Be a part of it
body.text: This analysis is the first to be published from the Historic Censuses Digitisation Project, as part of our statistical archaeology work. Your feedback and comments would be welcomed. Understanding what interests you and how you use or interpret the analysis will assist us with the production of data stories from the 1921 Census digitised data.

body.h2: Be a part of it
body.text: We’re continuing digitisation work with our partners at the University of Salford Pattern Recognition and Image Analysis Research Lab (PRImA) who have carried out innovative research and developed software tools and workflows to enable high quality digitisation of printed tabular statistics.

body.h2: Be a part of it
body.text: The digitisation process started with optical character recognition (OCR) of over 140,000 digital images of the small area statistics outputs held by the ONS. This process recognised over 95% of the characters and numbers contained within the images.

body.h2: Be a part of it
body.text: In an effort to extract the extra 5% of characters, the PRImA team used crowdsourcing via the citizen science platform [Zooniverse](https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/dataliberation/1961-census/about/research). Over 2,800 volunteers classified images by the submission of figures from the images presented to them, 5.5 million classifications in total.

body.h2: Be a part of it
body.text: Interactives are produced with thanks to the [National Library of Scotland](https://maps.nls.uk/), for the use of [historical maps](https://maps.nls.uk/projects/subscription-api/).

body.h2: Be a part of it
body.text: We’re currently working on 1921 county and topic report tables and other census years alongside the release of 2021 data next year. To find out more, [sign up for GovDelivery updates on our historical census work](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/UKONS/subscribers/new).
